text: An alert's text is a summary written by whoever built the rule -- it's not a verdict. Validating, scoping, and escalating are the three moves that turn that summary into a real decision: check whether the data actually supports the claim, figure out how far the activity reaches, and only then decide if it needs to go further. Skip any one of them and both of last lesson's failure modes become likely.

Validation means checking the raw data the alert is based on -- the actual log line, the actual authentication event, the actual process execution record -- not just trusting the label someone else wrote. Scoping comes next: once something's confirmed real, the question changes from what to do about this one alert to how far this goes, checking other hosts, accounts, or systems touched by the same activity, because the first alert is rarely the full picture.

Take a real example: a SIEM fires on a suspicious login from a new location. Validation confirms the login happened exactly as described and passed MFA on the first try -- details the alert summary never included. Scoping then checks other accounts from that IP range, finds none, but finds the same account accessing a file share it has never touched before.

That one scoping finding changes everything. An alert escalates to Tier 2 when it meets one of three criteria: the activity is confirmed malicious and needs a response beyond Tier 1's authority, the scope can't be fully determined with Tier 1's access, or the situation needs deeper tools like forensics or memory capture that sit outside Tier 1's normal toolset.

The login alone looked containable at Tier 1 -- it was the unfamiliar file-share access found during scoping that pushed this past Tier 1's authority. Next, Lesson 19 covers how to write that finding up clearly, so whoever picks up the case next doesn't have to redo the validation and scoping work from scratch.
